name: Curiosity's sky crane (Mars Science Laboratory descent stage)

location.note: Approximate debris-site marker near Curiosity's landing area; use the linked orbital imagery to identify the hardware.
location.name: Gale crater, about 650 m from where Curiosity landed

headline: The rocket crane that lowered Curiosity onto Mars, then flew off to crash on purpose
story: On 6 August 2012, a rocket-powered platform hovered above Gale crater and lowered the rover Curiosity on cables until its wheels touched the ground. NASA called it the sky crane. Once the rover was down, the cables were cut.

Its job done, the descent stage flew away and crashed at a safe distance, as it had been programmed to, about 650 meters from the rover. One of Curiosity's rear hazard cameras may even have caught a distant cloud of dust thrown up by the impact.

HiRISE photographed the crash site from orbit the next day: a dark scar where the sky crane hit, with possible pieces of it scattered nearby. Scientists have watched the scar ever since; by 2015 it was fading more slowly than predicted. The broken descent stage still lies there, in the crater where it set Curiosity down.

facts.label: Flew after setting the rover down
facts.value: About 650 m before hitting the ground

facts.label: Why it crashed
facts.value: On purpose: it was programmed to fly away from the rover

facts.label: Canadian connection
facts.value: The rover it lowered carries Canada's APXS spectrometer, led from the University of Guelph
